before.description: Distinct traditions investigate landscapes, human settlement, and environmental change. Human geography shapes Annales; environmental inquiry has additional roots in natural history and conservation.

after.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
after.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
after.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Paul Vidal de la Blache influences Febvre and Bloch; George Perkins Marsh, Man and Nature (1864), is an environmental precursor, not an Annales founder. Additional readings: Sauer, “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949).

representative_people.context: Investigates how human activity forms a region’s geographical individuality; engages Michelet’s national framing. His human geography is a resource for Annales, with the reception limits retained in the connection note.
representative_people.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

representative_people.context: Studies human modification of physical environments; a precursor to environmental inquiry, not an Annales founder.
representative_people.works: Man and Nature; or, Physical Geography as Modified by Human Action (1864)

representative_people.context: Treats landscapes as related physical and cultural forms with histories; challenges rigid explanations from physical conditions alone.
Conservationist whose ecological observation and teaching supplied one model for reading landscapes; Cronon later recalls workshops modeled on his course.

after.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme.

strands.title: Human modification of physical environments

strands.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949); Cronon’s retrospective afterword

before.label: Environmental history
before.description: Makes relations among humans and the nonhuman world central to explanation; connects ecology, material change, culture, and power.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977.

representative_people.context: Environmental history.
Environmental history.
Environmental history.
Environmental history.

before.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route.

after.label: Environmental history
after.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

representative_people.context: Argues that organisms accompanying Europeans helped transform environments and sustain settler expansion, particularly in temperate regions.
representative_people.works: Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986)

representative_people.context: Connects the Dust Bowl with agricultural capitalism as well as environmental conditions; this is a contested explanation, not the field’s unanimous account.
representative_people.works: Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); “The Dirty Thirties: A Study in Agricultural Capitalism” (1986)

representative_people.context: Brings feminist history of science into environmental inquiry; argues that mechanical conceptions of nature support new forms of control and capitalist development.
representative_people.works: The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980)

representative_people.context: Links colonial property and ecological change, city–hinterland commodity flows, and cultural ideas of wilderness. His later afterword criticizes schematic capitalism and uneven treatment of Indigenous and colonial sources in his first book.
representative_people.works: Changes in the Land (1983); Nature’s Metropolis (1991); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995)

representative_people.context: Ecological observation and conservation ethics precede the field’s later consolidation; Cronon identifies a landscape-training model drawn from Leopold.
With ecologist Madhav Gadgil, examines changing resource use, social conflict and resistance in Indian environmental history. Distinct from Ranajit Guha.
representative_people.works: With Madhav Gadgil, This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India (1992; UC Press edition 1993)

representative_people.context: Ecologist collaborating with Ramachandra Guha on resource-use systems and their social and political conflicts in India.
representative_people.works: With Ramachandra Guha, This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India (1992; UC Press edition 1993)

representative_people.context: Traces conservation ideas through colonial island settings and scientific networks; his geographical emphasis differs from histories of mainland African conservation.
representative_people.works: Green Imperialism: Colonial Expansion, Tropical Island Edens and the Origins of Environmentalism, 1600–1860 (1995)

representative_people.context: Examines South African conservation through the politics of Kruger National Park, racial power and Afrikaner nationalism.
representative_people.works: The Kruger National Park: A Social and Political History (1995)

representative_people.context: Adapts Crosby’s biological-conquest question to introduced grazing animals and social change in Mexico’s Valle del Mezquital, emphasizing places with continuing Indigenous populations.
representative_people.works: A Plague of Sheep: Environmental Consequences of the Conquest of Mexico (1994)

after.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship.

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange
strands.focus: Compare Crosby’s temperate settler environments with Melville’s explicit adaptation to grazing animals, land and continuing Indigenous populations in Mexico.
strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

geography.people: Reviewed Vidal and Marsh as different resources; added Sauer’s cultural landscape and Leopold’s ecological teaching. Roster remains a selective set of resources for historians, with wider critical geography explicitly queued.
geography.works_and_arguments: Filled Vidal’s empty work with Tableau (1903), retaining national framing and human regional activity. Replaced Marsh’s unsuitable inherited Durkheim roster citation with primary bibliographic and scholarly reception support. Added distinct Sauer and Leopold works.
geography.internal_distinctions: Added four approaches: regional individuality, human modification, physical/cultural landscape forms, and ecological landscape reading. No single programme or universal founder is inferred.
geography.incoming_connections: Added the specific Michelet-to-Vidal engagement from the opening of Tableau. Considered Sauer’s citation of Vidal within the parent approach without manufacturing a separate inter-field edge.
geography.outgoing_connections: Preserved the Annales influence claim and its explicit limitation concerning support for both founders. Strengthened the existing environmental-history contribution with Lowenthal on Marsh and Cronon’s acknowledgment of teaching modeled on Leopold.
geography.evidence_and_interpretation: Read primary openings and a scholarly retrospective, distinguishing consulted editions, transcriptions and reception. Sauer’s opening transcription is not collated against the scan; the full essay and broader disciplinary reception remain unreviewed.

environment.people: Reviewed the inherited Crosby, Worster, Merchant and Cronon selections; added Leopold as precursor, Melville on Mexico, Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha on India, Grove on colonial conservation networks and Carruthers on South Africa. Names have distinct explanatory roles; environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship remain a concrete breadth gap.
environment.works_and_arguments: Filled all four inherited empty works with dated readings and arguments. Cronon’s three works distinguish property, commodity flows and wilderness; Melville’s preface explicitly adapts Crosby. Publisher descriptions are not recorded as full-book checks.
environment.internal_distinctions: Added eight approaches distinguishing ecological exchange, agricultural capitalism, feminist science/nature, colonial property, urban hinterlands, Indian resource conflict, differing colonial conservation studies, and cultural wilderness. Retained disagreements and Cronon’s self-criticism.
environment.incoming_connections: Specified Marsh/Leopold resources and Merchant’s science connection. Added Cronon’s explicitly acknowledged use of anthropology for property analysis alongside economics and legal theory. Kept economic and technology affinities as comparisons.
environment.outgoing_connections: Specified Crosby/Melville/Grove in the global-history resource link and Merchant in feminist inquiry. Added Cronon’s cultural analysis and Carruthers’s South African book as contributions, not school-wide influence claims. Annales affinity remains undirected.
environment.evidence_and_interpretation: Consulted Cronon’s primary essay and retrospective, Melville’s indexed primary preface, Merchant’s scanned excerpt, scholarly reception and scoped publisher descriptions. Worster’s PDF returned 403; used repository abstract and annotated institutional bibliography within their limits. Critical reception and empirical disputes remain queued.

environment: Add a bounded environmental-justice and Indigenous-scholarship comparison within the pre-2001 scope; assess Robert Bullard and Indigenous-authored histories alongside the existing conservation and settler-landscape selections.
